pg006_n0004: This textbook, English for Secondary Schools, has been written specifically for Form One students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0005: The book has been prepared in accordance with the 2023 English Language Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I-IV, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg006_n0006: Some of the contents in this book have been adapted from English for Secondary Schools for Form One that was published in 2018 in accordance with the 2005 Ordinary Level Syllabus issued by the then Ministry of Education and Vocational Training (MoEVT).
pg006_n0008: The book consists of ten chapters, namely Using ICT tools to search for information, Listening to various types of information, Producing short and coherent oral messages, Developing vocabulary from conversations and written texts, Using appropriate grammar and vocabulary in oral and written contexts, Reading texts for comprehension, Comprehending oral messages, Responding through oral and written communication, Using appropriate grammar and vocabulary for oral communication and Creating a variety of texts using appropriate tone and register.
pg006_n0009: The book contains engaging exercises, real-life examples, and interactive activities that will help you develop the four basic language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing.
pg006_n0010: In addition, the book will help you expand your vocabulary through words and phrases that you will use in your everyday communication.
pg006_n0011: This will enable you to express yourself accurately and fluently in both oral and written forms.
pg006_n0013: Additional learning resources are available in the TIE e-Library at https://ol.tie.go.tz or ol.tie.go.tz
pg006_im002: QR code for additional learning resources from the TIE e-Library.

pg009_n0008: Lwaga woke up to the sounds of birds chirping.

pg009_n0010: He knew he was late for school.

pg009_n0013: When he managed to sit up, he held his head in his hands as if it were heavy.
pg009_n0015: “Where am I?” He muttered to himself.
pg009_n0017: He had been involved in a plane crash!
pg009_n0019: He had won a Geography Essay Competition on water preservation in Africa.
pg009_n0020: He was awarded together with other things, a paid trip to the Kingdom of Lesotho, a tiny landlocked country, bordered by South Africa.
pg009_n0021: He remembered his excitement to visit The Kingdom in the Sky, as it is famously known and see Katse Dam, the second largest dam in Africa.

pg010_n0004: He found himself alone in an unfamiliar place.

pg010_n0006: Amazingly, he found it in flight mode and the battery was at 37 per cent.
pg010_n0007: Although he was weak, he managed to change the phone to the normal mode and send an SOS to all his emergency contacts.
pg010_n0008: He pulled himself and started dragging himself to find out the signal.
pg010_n0009: After an hour he found a strong signal and looked for his location on the Google Maps.
pg010_n0010: He found out that he was in the middle of nowhere.
pg010_n0011: Immediately, he pinpointed his location on the map and tried to tap the button “share”.
pg010_n0012: He felt dizzy; as he was struggling to hold his phone, he lost consciousness.
pg010_n0013: When he regained consciousness, he realised that he was in hospital.
pg010_n0014: His legs and one arm were in casts as he had several broken bones.
pg010_n0015: Later they told him that the messages he had sent and the location he had shared helped the rescuers locate him.

pg015_n0003: Listening to various types of information
pg015_n0007: Listening is a very important skill in learning English since it enables a person to engage, understand, connect, sympathise and acquire knowledge and information from different sources.
pg015_n0008: In this chapter, you will learn to listen to and acquire information from presentations and answer questions accordingly.
pg015_n0009: You will then practise pronouncing and writing words heard from oral, audio and audio-visual sources.
pg015_n0010: Furthermore, you will learn to reproduce messages from oral presentations.
pg015_n0011: The competencies developed will help you to interpret oral messages and enhance your communication in various contexts.

pg031_n0058: The words in (a) are called minimal pairs.
pg031_n0059: Minimal pairs are pairs of words that vary in meaning by only one sound (phoneme) while sharing pronunciation in other sounds.
pg031_n0063: These words differ only in the first consonant sounds.
pg031_n0064: The word rice begins with the consonant /r/ while lice begins with the consonant /l/.
pg031_n0065: It is very important to get the pronunciation right because if you pronounce the word wrongly, you change the meaning completely.
pg031_n0069: These words differ only in vowel length.
pg031_n0070: In the word ship, ‘i’ is pronounced as the short vowel /ɪ/, while in the word sheep, ‘ee’ is pronounced as the long vowel /iː/.
pg031_n0073: These words differ only in the final consonant sounds.
pg031_n0074: The word pit ends with the consonant sound /t/ while the word pin ends with the consonant sound /n/.

pg033_im004_crop_v1: Activity 2: Practising pronunciation with proper word stress
pg033_n0012: Practising pronunciation with proper word stress
pg033_n0014: (a) Read the following text about stress.
pg033_n0015: Then, read the sentences containing words with stressed syllables below it.
pg033_n0017: When we pronounce a multi-syllable word, one of the syllables is pronounced with more prominence, and this is called a stressed syllable.
pg033_n0018: Stress, therefore, is the force used when saying a syllable in a word.
pg033_n0019: The other syllables in the word are pronounced with less emphasis and referred to as unstressed syllables.
pg033_n0023: proDUCE - He works on a farm and helps to proDUCE fresh vegetables.
pg033_n0024: PROduce - The local store sells a variety of fresh PROduce.
pg033_n0027: reCORD - She likes to reCORD her favourite songs on her phone.
pg033_n0028: REcord - The police officers have made a REcord of the crimes in our area.
pg033_n0031: inCREASE - The company plans to inCREASE its production capacity.
pg033_n0032: INcrease - There is an INcrease in the cost of running the business.
pg033_n0035: DEsert - The camel navigates through the hot DEsert.
pg033_n0036: deSERT - After a long wait, he decided to deSERT the company.
pg033_n0039: reJECT - The admissions committee decided to reJECT her application.
pg034_n0007: reFUND - He decided to reFUND the money he had borrowed from his friend.
pg034_n0008: REfund - The store issued a REfund for the damaged item.
pg034_n0012: PERmit - The city requires a PERmit for building construction.
pg034_n0013: perMIT - They perMIT their children to participate in sports.
pg034_n0015: In each sentence, the capitalised syllables are pronounced with stress.
pg034_n0016: The difference in stress of the syllables result in the difference in meaning.
pg034_n0017: For example, if the word produced is stressed on the first syllable (PROduce), it means fruits and vegetables, but when it is stressed on the second syllable (proDUCE), it means creating or making something.
pg034_n0018: Therefore, stress is important in distinguishing meanings and conveying accurate messages.

pg036_n0005: In English, short vowels are single vowel sounds that are pronounced shortly and clearly.
pg036_n0006: Apart from sound /æ/, other short vowels in English include the following:
pg036_n0010: Short e /e/ or /ɛ/, as in bed, red, pen, step, bet

pg036_n0016: Short o /ɒ/ or /ɑ/, as in dog, top, pot, log, box

pg046_n0007: Vocabulary is an essential part of English language learning.
pg046_n0008: This chapter will enable you to acquire enough vocabulary through speaking and writing activities.

pg046_n0010: You will, therefore, learn new vocabulary in conversations and written texts.

pg046_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to communicate well in speech and writing.

pg047_n0005: Read and act out the following dialogue and answer the questions that follow.
pg047_n0008: Mfwimi lives in Igagala Village, Njombe District and Balongage lives in Maduma Village, Mufindi District.
pg047_n0009: One day Balongage, visited his friend Mfwimi.
pg047_n0010: Mfwimi took him to his avocado farm.
pg047_n0011: They had a conversation as follows:]
pg047_n0014: Welcome to my green gold farm, my friend.
pg047_n0017: [Admiring the trees] Green gold! My friend, this is a new term to me.
pg047_n0021: We call it so here because it is the major selling crop in Njombe.
pg047_n0022: Many people here in Njombe have stories of success to tell about this crop.
pg047_n0026: Your avocado trees look very healthy.
pg047_n0027: How do you take care of them?
pg047_n0031: It all starts with selecting good avocado seedlings.
pg047_n0032: I also use organic manure to enrich the soil before planting the seedlings.
pg047_n0033: Moreover, I use balanced fertiliser to boost growth and yield the best fruits.
pg047_n0039: Weeding is very important to prevent the avocado trees from being attacked by pests and diseases.
pg047_n0040: Some farmers use chemicals, but I prefer hand weeding.
pg047_n0041: My wife and I do the weeding using hand hoes.
pg047_n0042: We sometimes hire people to help us.
pg047_n0045: Do you face any challenges growing avocado seedlings?
pg047_n0049: The biggest challenge is during the dry season when I use a traditional watering can to water the
pg048_n0004: seedlings, and that is quite a task.
pg048_n0005: I’m thinking of shifting to drip irrigation.
pg048_n0008: So, after all the hard work, how long does it take before the harvest?
pg048_n0011: [Pointing at avocados] You can see some are ready now.
pg048_n0012: It usually takes a few years for avocado trees to start bearing fruits, but once they start, you can harvest them annually.
pg048_n0013: It is recommended to pick them when they are mature and not when they are ripe.
pg048_n0017: I want to start my avocado farm.
pg048_n0018: Can you help me to get started, please?
pg048_n0022: I have a few healthy seedlings that I can sell to you.
pg048_n0023: I will also accompany you to the local nursery here in Njombe where you can buy some too.
pg048_n0027: Sorry, I forgot to ask you about the market.
pg048_n0030: [Smiling] My friend, that is why we call it green gold.
pg048_n0031: Avocados are very marketable in the country and abroad.
pg048_n0033: You don’t need to worry about their market as long as your avocados are healthy.
pg048_n0034: For your information, Tanzania is one of the largest producers of avocados in Africa.
pg048_n0037: Is there anything important I have not asked?
pg048_n0042: You need to remove all the withered leaves to promote healthy growth.
pg049_n0003: Thank you, Mr Green Gold. [They both burst into laughter at Mfwimi’s nickname]
pg049_n0006: You’re welcome, Balongage! Good luck with your avocado farming!
pg049_n0007: If you need any more tips or help with your farm, don’t hesitate to ask.
pg049_n0009: [The following day, Balongage left Mfwimi’s home very determined to turn his small maize farm into an avocado farm.
pg049_n0010: Although he faced some challenges, he never gave up.
pg049_n0011: His dedication and resilience brought him the success he had never imagined.]

pg051_n0006: A debate is a discussion whereby individuals express their arguments by focusing on a specific topic or idea.
pg051_n0007: Usually, in a school context, a debate involves two sides or teams: one supporting a proposition (the affirmative team), and one opposing a proposition (the opposing team).
pg051_n0008: However, there should be a debate leadership to ensure the quality of evidence, argument and the performance of the debate, hence making a judgement.
pg051_n0009: The leaders of a debate include a chairperson, a secretary and a timekeeper.
pg051_n0010: Sometimes, in the school context, the judgement may be done by a teacher.
pg051_n0011: The winner is the one who gets the highest points.
pg051_n0012: The floor (audience) may be involved in the debate, but they will not be directly engaged in the discussion.

pg052_n0016: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.
pg052_n0020: Seaweed cultivation in Zanzibar involves a simple and natural process.
pg052_n0021: First, farmers tie small pieces of seaweed to ropes.
pg052_n0022: These ropes are then placed in the shallow, clean water surrounding the island.
pg052_n0023: Over a few weeks, the seaweed grows in the ocean’s gentle embrace.
pg052_n0024: Healthy seaweed often has vibrant colours and looks fresh and plump.
pg052_n0025: Once it is ready, the farmers harvest it by hand.
pg052_im001: Five women in shallow sea water cultivate and harvest seaweed by hand.
pg053_n0003: It is commonly used in various cuisines, including soups and salads, as seasoning.
pg053_n0004: Seaweed extracts are often used in cosmetics and skincare products.
pg053_n0005: They can help hydrate the skin and are rich in vitamins and minerals.
pg053_n0006: Seaweed can be processed into organic fertilisers.
pg053_n0007: These fertilisers provide essential nutrients to plants and improve soil quality.
pg053_n0008: In medicine, seaweed is used to make some pills that might help sick people to feel better.
pg053_n0009: Even in packaging, seaweed is used to make things that will not damage the environment.
pg053_n0010: Seaweed can also be used in the production of biofuels as an alternative to fossil fuels.
pg053_n0011: Moreover, seaweed farming is eco-friendly, as it doesn’t require harmful chemicals or deforestation.

pg074_n0025: Read the following text and take note of the italicised words.
pg074_n0027: It was just recently that Ambilike discovered that he was almost running out of money.
pg074_n0028: Initially, he was in a boarding school, so he did not have to buy his food for the whole year.
pg074_n0029: He had just moved to an apartment and decided to go to a nearby market and buy an apple, a mango, two bananas, one kilogram of meat, and a small bag of maize flour.
pg074_n0030: When he found out that the money he had could not pay for all the things he wanted, he returned the bag of maize flour and paid for the rest of the things.
pg075_n0004: The italicised words are called articles.
pg075_n0005: Articles are words used before nouns to provide information about such nouns.
pg075_n0006: They help to specify whether the noun is referring to something specific or general.
pg075_n0007: There are three main articles in English: a, an and the.
pg075_n0008: These articles can be grouped into two: indefinite and definite articles.
pg075_n0012: Indefinite articles, a and an are used before singular nouns to refer to any member of a group.
pg075_n0013: An is used in the following contexts:
pg075_n0017: before a singular word that begins with a vowel (e.g. an apple, an egg, an order).
pg075_n0020: before words beginning with silent h ( e.g. an hour, an heir).
pg075_n0021: A is used before words that begin with a consonant sound.
pg075_n0022: NB: The article a is also used with words that begin with a vowel which is pronounced like consonant y (e.g. a university, a European, a unit).
pg075_n0025: The definite article, the, is used before a singular or plural noun to indicate that the identity of the noun is known, or a noun has been mentioned earlier in the same text.
pg075_n0030: The car in the garage is mine (the is used to indicate a specific, as opposed to any other car).
pg075_n0033: I saw a dog in the park.
pg075_n0034: The dog was chasing a ball. (the is used in the second mention to refer to the specific dog that was introduced earlier.

pg077_n0067: The words that have been replaced in the sentences and passages are called nouns and the new words are called pronouns.
pg077_n0068: Pronouns are used to replace nouns that have already been mentioned or nouns that do not need to be specifically named.
pg077_n0069: They help to communicate effectively and avoid repetition in speech and writing.
pg077_n0070: The chart that follows summarises the types, definitions and examples of pronouns.
pg078_n0019: They are used to refer to specific individuals or things.
pg078_n0030: They point to specific things or people in a sentence.
pg078_n0041: mine, yours, his, their, hers, its, ours, theirs
pg078_n0048: They are used when the subject and object of a sentence are the same person or thing.
pg078_n0049: They show that the action in a sentence goes back to the same person or thing.

pg092_n0007: She loved sleeping more than anything else.
pg092_n0008: Hence, she always arrived late at school.
pg092_n0009: Every morning, her mother would wake her up, but Aika would go back to sleep; Aika’s mother tried everything, but nothing worked.
pg092_n0010: So, that was her life for sometime.
pg092_n0012: Firstly, her mornings would start in chaos as she would rush to get dressed and have a quick breakfast.
pg092_n0013: She would get out of the house and find herself running like a cheetah through the streets to make it to school on time.
pg092_n0014: On the way, she would collide with other people and cause mayhem.
pg092_n0015: Moreover, she would sometimes step into Machinga’s goods as she ran.
pg092_n0016: This behaviour caused a lot of problems for her.
pg092_n0017: Sometimes people would grab her hand and ask her to pay for the damage.
pg092_n0018: However, other people around would defend her, so she would be let off.
pg092_n0020: Next, her teachers and classmates would be astonished as she burst into the classroom, panting and untidy.
pg092_n0021: Her English teacher, Ms Mpingo, would raise an eyebrow and say, “Aika, it is nice of you to join us again.”
pg092_n0022: Ms Mpingo knew Aika needed to learn the importance of punctuality.
pg092_n0023: So, together with Aika’s classmates, they appointed Aika class monitor.
pg092_n0024: One of her responsibilities was to do a class roll call and report to her class teacher.
pg092_n0025: Therefore, this role made Aika punctual.
pg092_n0026: It was not easy at first but she decided to change her schedule.
pg092_n0027: She would set her alarm for 5:30 am and lay out her school uniform and the school bag the night before.
pg092_n0028: She would even ask her family to take breakfast together as a motivation to wake up early.
pg092_n0030: Finally, Aika’s unpunctuality became a thing of the past.
pg092_n0031: She discovered that being punctual not only reduced her stress levels but it also allowed her to be more attentive in class and build better relationships with her classmates.

pg099_n0011: He was the chief of the Jukuns, a brave and warlike tribe, and they waged war on the peace-loving Igala people.
pg099_n0012: At that time, the Igala people were ruled by a very beautiful queen, whose name was Ebule-Jonu.
pg099_n0013: She was a good and just ruler.
pg099_n0014: All her people loved her very much.

pg099_n0016: For this reason, they had to fight.
pg099_n0018: The situation became more and more serious, and the fighting grew fiercer and fiercer.
pg099_n0019: Every evening, the women of Igala wept, as their husbands, sons, and lovers returned from the battle exhausted and wounded, or when some did not return at all.
pg099_n0020: Many plans were made, but they brought no success.
pg099_n0022: Her councillors wanted to seek the advice of a learned soothsayer who lived in the desert.
pg099_n0023: Ebule-Jonu wanted her people to win the war on their own without asking for advice.
pg099_n0024: At last, however, she allowed the councillors to go.
pg099_n0026: They travelled with great care because their journey led them through their enemies’ camps.
pg099_n0027: It was there where the youngest councillor lost his life.
pg099_n0028: He drew attention to himself while the eldest councillor led the others to safety.
pg099_n0029: They went on sorrowfully through the hot and dry desert until, at last, they reached the

pg100_n0005: They travelled back home quickly, and even more sadly than before because of the soothsayer’s words.

pg104_n0024: Retelling a story means presenting the story you have read or heard without leaving out key information or adding irrelevant information.
pg104_n0025: It enables one to develop recalling, sequencing and imagination skills.
pg104_n0026: Moreover, it facilitates one’s building of vocabulary and strengthening of comprehension skills.
pg104_n0027: It also prepares one for successful writing, critical thinking and communication.
pg104_n0029: Here are some techniques for a successful retelling of a story.
pg104_n0033: Identify and put the main events in order.
pg104_n0034: This involves knowing the flow of events (plot).
pg104_n0037: Use the “first, next, then, last” formula.
pg104_n0038: In retelling the story, one needs to have a structure through which he or she will organise the story from what happened first, how the events of the story developed and what happened last as the story got to the end.
pg104_n0041: Map the story before retelling it by visualising it or understanding it so that you break it into key elements (characters, setting, plot, setting, conflict, and resolution).
pg104_n0042: Mapping a story helps one to understand and remember the events.
pg104_n0045: Focus on the plot structure (elements) exposition, rising action, climax, falling action or resolution to enable you to sequence the events.
pg104_n0048: Practise retelling the story in a pair or group.
pg104_n0049: Listen to each other’s story, encourage one another and learn from others.
pg104_n0050: This will help you learn how to retell a story to others.

pg108_n0032: Let's start with the meaning of paraphrasing.
pg108_n0033: It means using your own words to express a speech or text clearly without changing its original meaning.
pg108_n0034: For instance, the sentence “She has been fond of watching games since she was young” simply can be paraphrased as “She has been enjoying watching games since her childhood”

pg109_n0019: Paraphrasing can be done using the synonyms; for example, important can be paraphrased as significant.
pg109_n0020: It can also be done through the change of voice, and vice versa.
pg109_n0021: For example, the sentence “The chef prepared delicious food” can be paraphrased as “Delicious food was prepared by the chef.”

pg109_n0037: Paraphrasing complex text requires some steps.

pg120_n0017: A phone conversation is a common way to communicate with various people.
pg120_n0018: The conversation may be formal or informal, depending on who you are communicating with.
pg120_n0019: It is important to understand the difference between formal and informal phone conversations for effective communication.
pg120_n0020: The following table highlights some of the differences:
pg120_n0033: It is used for official purposes, including doing job interviews, contacting authorities, and reporting official issues.
pg120_n0035: It is used for casual, personal and friendly interactions, with family friends and colleagues.
pg120_n0040: It uses formal language, and it is a polite and respectful interaction.
pg120_n0042: It uses informal language and it is a relaxed and friendly interaction.
pg120_n0048: It begins with formal greetings and states the name, place and the purpose of the call.
pg120_n0049: For example Good afternoon! My name is Sadala Nova from Kurunzi in Mpome ward.
pg120_n0051: It starts with casual greetings and conversation with a friendly question or statement such as Hi or Hey.
pg121_n0015: It flows professionally and asks for clarification if needed.
pg121_n0016: It also, uses polite expressions such as Could you have something else to share or Could you please repeat that? or I’m sorry, I didn’t catch that.
pg121_n0018: It can flow naturally without a specific agenda.
pg121_n0019: It is for sharing personal updates, asking about the other person’s day, and engaging in small talk.
pg121_n0024: It ends by summarising the main points discussed, thanking the person for their time, and offering contact information if necessary.
pg121_n0026: It ends up casually with informal closing statements such as Goodbye! Take care Keep in touch etc.
pg121_n0028: Consider language, communication skills and whether the context of the call is formal or informal to maintain a positive relationship and achieve the purpose of the conversation.

pg136_n0006: Nonverbal cues are very important in communication because they convey emotions, attitudes and intentions without the use of words.
pg136_n0007: They include various aspects of body language, facial expressions, gestures, vocal tones and other signals that are expressed through body movements and actions.
pg136_n0008: It is important, however, to remember that nonverbal cues can vary significantly across cultures, and therefore, interpreting them correctly requires sensitivity and cultural awareness.
pg136_n0009: Study the following nonverbal cues and their characteristics.
pg136_n0024: Showing emotions and attitudes through smiling, frowning, raising eyebrows, or squinting
pg136_n0031: Maintaining or avoiding eye contact during a conversation it shows confidence, interest, or discomfort.
pg136_n0038: How individuals hold themselves (e.g., slouching, standing up) indicates their level of engagement, openness, or authority.
pg136_n0045: Enhancing or clarifying verbal messages through pointing, waving, or using thumbs up
pg136_n0052: Physical touch, such as a handshake, hug, or pat on the back communicates feelings of warmth, sympathy, or support.
pg136_n0059: The tone, pitch, and volume of someone’s voice reveals emotions (e.g., anger, and excitement) and influence the meaning of spoken words.
pg136_n0066: How individuals dress and present themselves. It can convey their personality, social status, or cultural affiliations.
pg136_n0073: The absence of speech can be a powerful nonverbal cue for conveying emotions like confusion, discomfort, or respect.
pg136_im004: Table of nonverbal cues and their characteristics: 1. facial expression—showing emotions and attitudes through smiling, frowning, raising eyebrows, or squinting; 2. eye contact—maintaining or avoiding eye contact during a conversation shows confidence, interest, or discomfort; 3. body posture—how individuals hold themselves, such as slouching or standing up, indicates engagement, openness, or authority; 4. gestures—enhancing or clarifying verbal messages through pointing, waving, or using thumbs up; 5. touch—physical touch such as a handshake, hug, or pat on the back communicates warmth, sympathy, or support; 6. vocal cues—the tone, pitch, and volume of someone’s voice reveal emotions and influence the meaning of spoken words; 7. clothing and appearance—how individuals dress and present themselves can convey personality, social status, or cultural affiliations; 8. silence—the absence of speech can convey emotions such as confusion, discomfort, or respect.

pg164_n0003: Creating a variety of texts using appropriate tone and register
pg164_n0007: In creating various texts, tone and register are of utmost significance.
pg164_n0008: Tone refers to the attitude or feelings you have about the topic you intend to write on while register is the level of formality or the use of language according to the context.
pg164_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn the main stages of writing texts.
pg164_n0010: Next, you will learn how to write friendly letters and invitations.
pg164_n0011: Thirdly, you will learn how to create dialogues on various topics.
pg164_n0012: Thereafter, you will learn how to create and express your daily and weekly routines orally.
pg164_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to create a variety of texts using appropriate tone and register according to the context.

pg164_n0023: Recognising the main stages in writing texts
pg165_n0002: (a) Read the following dialogue and then answer the questions that follow.
pg165_n0003: [One Saturday evening, Mnaya and his friend Hida met at the school cafeteria for refreshments. While having some drinks, they shared various issues.]
pg165_n0006: Hida, I’ve been struggling with my writing lately.
pg165_n0007: It just doesn’t seem to flow the way I want it to.
pg165_n0010: Writing a text is like preparing a special meal.
pg165_n0011: You need a good recipe to cook delicious food.
pg165_n0012: Similarly, in writing a good text, you need to follow some steps.
pg165_n0019: The stages are prewriting, drafting, revising, editing and proofreading.
pg165_n0023: Prewriting is like collecting ingredients for my special meal.
pg165_n0027: In writing, prewriting involves gathering the materials, organising your thoughts and planning your writing.
pg165_n0028: This is the foundation for your writing.
pg165_n0031: Could drafting be like when I start cooking my special meal?
pg165_n0035: Drafting involves putting your ideas in written form.
pg165_n0036: Just let your creativity flow and get the words down on paper as a professional chef’s first attempt at preparing a meal.
pg165_n0040: The next step is like adjusting the flavours and spices in a meal to make it test good, right?
pg165_n0044: This is like revising in writing where you go back and check your draft critically just like what the chef does to improve the taste of the meal.
pg165_n0045: It involves reviewing and improving the draft.
pg165_n0046: This should be followed by editing which involves polishing the writing to make it error-free!
pg166_n0002: Check for grammar, spelling, punctuation, consistency and arrangement of sentences.
pg166_n0005: So, I consider proofreading to be like tasting the food before serving it, right?
pg166_n0009: Proofreading is the final step like the last tasting before the meal leaves the kitchen.
pg166_n0010: Therefore, you need to review the whole text, line by line, to identify and correct any grammatical errors and spelling mistakes.
pg166_n0013: Writing a good text is indeed like cooking a meal.
pg166_n0014: Each step plays a crucial role in writing.
pg166_n0015: I’m so excited because my struggling days with writing are over.
pg166_n0021: [Mnaya smiles, feeling inspired and ready to start his writing with a new understanding of the steps in writing]

pg178_n0016: [Nyenza, Jamal and Manjana are friends who meet after school for daily discussion.

pg178_n0020: [With enthusiasm he greets everyone] Hello, guys!

pg178_n0030: It’s good to see you, man.
pg178_n0031: Back to today’s business; what are we discussing today?
pg178_n0034: We agreed to talk about the environment.
pg179_n0005: Okay! Who can tell us the meaning of environment?
pg179_n0008: If I can chip in quickly, I believe it is everything around us - the air we breathe, the water we drink, the land we cultivate, animals, even the trees we are sitting under right now.
pg179_n0012: Our environment consists of all things and their surroundings.
pg179_n0013: So it’s important to protect it.
pg179_n0020: Our survival depends on the environment.
pg179_n0021: It provides us with resources like food, clean water, and shelter.
pg179_n0022: So, if we don’t stop destroying it, we’ll perish!
pg179_n0026: Our economy relies heavily on agriculture and tourism, both depend on a healthy environment.
pg179_n0027: Protecting our forests, rivers and wildlife will continue to attract more tourists.
pg179_n0031: But I’ve heard about issues that destroy the environment.
pg179_n0036: There are challenges we face and the biggest of all is deforestation.
pg179_n0037: People cut down trees for firewood without replanting, new ones, leading to soil erosion.
pg179_n0040: Another challenge is pollution from industrial waste, plastic, and even the air we breathe.
pg179_n0041: I think this is the biggest threat.
pg179_n0045: I have seen how soil erosion has reduced our food production.
pg179_n0046: Also, the use of chemicals has contaminated the groundwater.
pg179_n0049: So we have all these challenges, but how do we overcome them?
pg180_n0005: I think the government should implement policies to promote environmental conservation.
pg180_n0009: However, we all need to be part of the solution by conserving water, reducing waste, and using energy wisely.
pg180_n0010: Together, we can protect our environment for future generations.
pg180_n0013: [Smiles] There’s a lot we can do, Jamal.
pg180_n0014: We should also promote tree planting and reforestation.
pg180_n0015: Additionally, we need to educate others about environmental issues.
pg180_n0018: [Inspired] I’m going to start by planting more trees in our village and teaching others about caring for the environment.
pg180_n0025: Does anyone have anything more to share before we end our discussion?
pg180_n0034: Thank you all for the fruitful discussion.

pg006_n0004_easy_read: This textbook, English for Secondary Schools, is for Form One students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0005_easy_read:
The Ministry of Education, Science and Technology issued the 2023 English Language Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I-IV.
This book follows that syllabus.
pg006_n0006_easy_read:
Some content in this book comes from English for Secondary Schools for Form One.
That book was published in 2018.
It followed the 2005 Ordinary Level Syllabus issued by the Ministry of Education and Vocational Training (MoEVT) at that time.
pg006_n0008_easy_read:
The book has 10 chapters:
- Using ICT tools to search for information
- Listening to various types of information
- Producing short and clear oral messages
- Developing vocabulary from conversations and written texts
- Using appropriate grammar and vocabulary in oral and written contexts
- Reading texts for comprehension
- Understanding oral messages
- Responding through oral and written communication
- Using appropriate grammar and vocabulary for oral communication
- Creating a variety of texts using appropriate tone and register
pg006_n0009_easy_read:
The book has:
- engaging exercises
- real-life examples
- interactive activities
These will help you develop 4 basic language skills:
- listening
- speaking
- reading
- writing
pg006_n0010_easy_read:
The book will also help you learn more vocabulary.
You will learn words and phrases for everyday communication.
pg006_n0011_easy_read: This will help you express yourself clearly and fluently in speaking and writing.
pg006_n0013_easy_read: You can find more learning resources in the TIE e-Library at https://ol.tie.go.tz or ol.tie.go.tz

- find reliable learning materials

pg030_n0021_easy_read: Telling apart words that sound very similar but have different meanings
pg031_n0058_easy_read: The words in (a) are called minimal pairs.
pg031_n0059_easy_read:
Minimal pairs are 2 words.
They have different meanings because 1 sound is different.
The other sounds stay the same.
pg031_n0063_easy_read: These words are different only in the first consonant sound.
pg031_n0064_easy_read:
The word rice starts with the consonant sound /r/.
The word lice starts with the consonant sound /l/.
pg031_n0065_easy_read:
It is very important to say words correctly.
If you say a word the wrong way, the meaning changes completely.
pg031_n0069_easy_read: These words are different only in vowel length.
pg031_n0070_easy_read:
In the word ship, "i" is the short vowel /ɪ/.
In the word sheep, "ee" is the long vowel /iː/.
pg031_n0073_easy_read: These words are different only in the final consonant sound.
pg031_n0074_easy_read:
The word pit ends with the consonant sound /t/.
The word pin ends with the consonant sound /n/.

pg075_n0004_easy_read: The words in italics are called articles.
pg075_n0005_easy_read:
Articles are words that come before nouns.

English has 3 main articles:
- a
- an
- the
pg075_n0008_easy_read:
These articles are in 2 groups:
- indefinite articles
- definite articles
pg075_n0012_easy_read:
The indefinite articles are a and an.
We use them before singular nouns to mean any member of a group.
pg075_n0013_easy_read: We use an in these cases:
pg075_n0017_easy_read:
before a singular word that begins with a vowel, for example:
- an apple
- an egg
- an order
pg075_n0020_easy_read:
before words that begin with a silent h, for example:
- an hour
- an heir
pg075_n0021_easy_read: We use a before words that begin with a consonant sound.
pg075_n0022_easy_read:
Note:
We also use a before words that begin with a vowel letter but sound like the consonant y, for example:
- a university
- a European
- a unit
pg075_n0025_easy_read:
The definite article is the.
We use the before a singular or plural noun when the identity of the noun is known.
We also use the when the noun was mentioned earlier in the same text.

The car in the garage is mine.

Nonverbal cues are very important in communication.
They show emotions, attitudes, and intentions without words.
pg136_n0007_easy_read:
Nonverbal cues include:
- body language
- facial expressions
- gestures
- vocal tones
- other signals shown through body movements and actions
pg136_n0008_easy_read:
It is important to remember this:
Nonverbal cues can be very different across cultures.
So, people need sensitivity and cultural awareness to understand them correctly.
pg136_n0009_easy_read: Study these nonverbal cues and their characteristics.
pg136_n0024_easy_read:
People show emotions and attitudes by:
- smiling
- frowning
- raising their eyebrows
- squinting
pg136_n0031_easy_read:
In a conversation, a person may keep eye contact or avoid it.
This can show confidence, interest, or discomfort.
pg136_n0038_easy_read: How people hold their bodies, for example by slouching or standing up straight, can show their level of engagement, openness, or authority.
pg136_n0045_easy_read:
Gestures can support or make spoken messages clearer.
Examples are:
- pointing
- waving
- using thumbs up
pg136_n0052_easy_read: Physical touch, such as a handshake, hug, or pat on the back, can show warmth, sympathy, or support.
pg136_n0059_easy_read:
The tone, pitch, and volume of a person's voice can show emotions, such as anger and excitement.
They can also change the meaning of spoken words.
pg136_n0066_easy_read:
How people dress and present themselves can show:
- personality
- social status
- cultural affiliations
pg136_n0073_easy_read:
Not speaking can be a strong nonverbal cue.
It can show emotions such as confusion, discomfort, or respect.

pg165_n0045_easy_read: Revising means reviewing and improving the draft.
